en.content: The mass of $$\mathrm{AgCl}$$ precipitated when a solution containing $$11.70 \mathrm{~g}$$ of $$\mathrm{NaCl}$$ is added to a solution containing $$3.4 \mathrm{~g}$$ of $$\mathrm{AgNO}_3$$ is [Atomic mass of $$\mathrm{Ag}=108$$, Atomic mass of $$\mathrm{Na}=23$$]
en.explanation:
To determine the mass of $$\mathrm{AgCl}$$ precipitated, we need to analyze the reaction between $$\mathrm{NaCl}$$ and $$\mathrm{AgNO}_3$$. The balanced chemical equation for the reaction is:

$$\mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{AgNO}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl} + \mathrm{NaNO}_3$$

From the equation, we can see that one mole of $$\mathrm{NaCl}$$ reacts with one mole of $$\mathrm{AgNO}_3$$ to produce one mole of $$\mathrm{AgCl}$$.

First, we need to find the number of moles of $$\mathrm{NaCl}$$ and $$\mathrm{AgNO}_3$$ present in the given masses.

The molar mass of $$\mathrm{NaCl}$$ is:

$$\mathrm{M_{NaCl}} = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 \, \mathrm{g/mol}$$

So, the number of moles of $$\mathrm{NaCl}$$ in $$11.70 \, \mathrm{g}$$ is:

$$\mathrm{n_{NaCl}} = \frac{11.70 \, \mathrm{g}}{58.5 \, \mathrm{g/mol}} = 0.20 \, \mathrm{mol}$$

The molar mass of $$\mathrm{AgNO}_3$$ is:

$$\mathrm{M_{AgNO_3}} = 108 + 14 + (3 \times 16) = 108 + 14 + 48 = 170 \, \mathrm{g/mol}$$

So, the number of moles of $$\mathrm{AgNO}_3$$ in $$3.4 \, \mathrm{g}$$ is:

$$\mathrm{n_{AgNO_3}} = \frac{3.4 \, \mathrm{g}}{170 \, \mathrm{g/mol}} = 0.02 \, \mathrm{mol}$$

Since the ratio of $$\mathrm{NaCl}$$ to $$\mathrm{AgNO}_3$$ in the reaction is 1:1, the limiting reagent is $$\mathrm{AgNO}_3$$, because it has fewer moles (0.02 moles) compared to $$\mathrm{NaCl}$$ (0.20 moles).

Now, we calculate the mass of $$\mathrm{AgCl}$$ produced from 0.02 moles of $$\mathrm{AgNO}_3$$.

The molar mass of $$\mathrm{AgCl}$$ is:

$$\mathrm{M_{AgCl}} = 108 + 35.5 = 143.5 \, \mathrm{g/mol}$$

So, the mass of $$\mathrm{AgCl}$$ produced from 0.02 moles is:

$$\mathrm{m_{AgCl}} = 0.02 \, \mathrm{mol} \times 143.5 \, \mathrm{g/mol} = 2.87 \, \mathrm{g}$$

Therefore, the mass of $$\mathrm{AgCl}$$ precipitated is 2.87 g, making the correct answer:

Option C: 2.87 g

en.content: Relative lowering of vapour pressure of a dilute solution of glucose dissolved in $$1 \mathrm{~kg}$$ of water is 0.002 . The molality of the solution is
en.explanation:
Relative lowering of vapor pressure is defined as:

$$ \frac{p^0 - p}{p^0} $$

For dilute solutions, this can be approximated by Raoult's law:

$$ \frac{p^0 - p}{p^0} = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{n_{\text{solvent}}} $$

Given that the relative lowering of vapor pressure is 0.002:

$$ 0.002 = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{n_{\text{solvent}}} $$

Since the solvent is water, with $ 1 \mathrm{~kg} $ of water:

$$ n_{\text{solvent}} = \frac{1000}{18} \approx 55.56 \, \text{mol} $$

Let $ n_{\text{solute}} $ be the moles of glucose. Then:

$$ 0.002 = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{55.56} $$

Solving for $ n_{\text{solute}} $:

$$ n_{\text{solute}} = 0.002 \times 55.56 \approx 0.111 \, \text{mol} $$

The molality (m) is defined as moles of solute per kilogram of solvent:

$$ \text{Molality} = \frac{0.111 \, \text{mol}}{1 \, \text{kg}} = 0.111 \, \text{m} $$

Therefore, the correct answer is:

Option C: 0.111

en.content: 1L of $$2 \mathrm{M~CH}_3 \mathrm{COOH}$$ is mixed with 1L of $$3 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{~C}_2 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{OH}$$ to form an ester. The rate of the reaction with respect to the initial rate when each solution is diluted with an equal volume of water will be
en.explanation:
When 1 L of $$2 \mathrm{M}~\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}$$ is mixed with 1 L of $$3 \mathrm{M}~\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{OH}$$, the total volume of the solution is 2 L.

The initial concentrations of the reactants before dilution are:

$$[\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}] = 2 \, \mathrm{M}$$

$$[\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{OH}] = 3 \, \mathrm{M}$$

After diluting each of these solutions with an equal volume of water (1 L), the final volume of each solution becomes 2 L. The new concentrations are:

$$\left[\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}\right] = \frac{2 \, \mathrm{M}}{2} = 1 \, \mathrm{M}$$

$$\left[\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{OH}\right] = \frac{3 \, \mathrm{M}}{2} = 1.5 \, \mathrm{M}$$

If the reaction is first-order with respect to both acetic acid ($\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}$) and ethanol ($\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{OH}$), the rate law is given by:

$$\text{Rate} = k \cdot [\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}] \cdot [\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{OH}]$$

Let the initial rate be:

$$\text{Initial Rate} = k \cdot 2 \, \mathrm{M} \cdot 3 \, \mathrm{M} = 6k$$

The rate after dilution is:

$$\text{New Rate} = k \cdot 1 \, \mathrm{M} \cdot 1.5 \, \mathrm{M} = 1.5k$$

The ratio of the new rate to the initial rate is:

$$\frac{\text{New Rate}}{\text{Initial Rate}} = \frac{1.5k}{6k} = \frac{1.5}{6} = 0.25$$

Therefore, the rate of the reaction with respect to the initial rate when each solution is diluted with an equal volume of water will be:

Option A: 0.25 times

$$\text { Let } A=\left[\begin{array}{ccc} 2 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 3 \end{array}\right]$$

For applying row operations $$A=I A$$, where $$A$$ is an identity matrix of order 3.

i.e. $$\left[\begin{array}{ccc}2 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 3\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{lll}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right] A$$

On applying $$R_1 \rightarrow \frac{R_1}{2}$$, we get

$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 5 / 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 3 \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{lll} \frac{1}{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right] A$$

$$\begin{aligned} & \text { On applying } R_3 \rightarrow R_3+R_1, \\ & \qquad\left[\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 5 / 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 5 / 2 & 3 \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ccc} 1 / 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 / 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right] A \end{aligned}$$

On applying $$R_1 \rightarrow R_1-\frac{5}{2} R_2, R_3 \rightarrow R_3-\frac{5}{2} R_2$$, we get

en.content: The frequency of an alternating current is $$50 \mathrm{~Hz}$$. What is the minimum time taken by current to reach its peak value from rms value?
en.explanation:
Given, Frequency of an alternating current, $$f=50 \mathrm{~Hz}$$

If $$t_1$$ be the time at rms value of alternating current, then

$$\begin{aligned} & I_{\mathrm{rms}}=I_0 \sin \omega t_1 \text { or } \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}=I_0 \sin \omega t_1 \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\sin \omega t_1 \Rightarrow \sin \frac{\pi}{4}=\sin \omega t_1 \Rightarrow t_1=\frac{\pi}{4 \omega} \quad \text{.... (i)} \end{aligned}$$

Similarly, If $$t_2$$ be time at peak value of alternating current, then $$I_0=I_0 \sin \omega t_2$$

$$\begin{aligned} 1 & =\sin \omega t_2 \\ \sin \frac{\pi}{2} & =\sin \omega t_2 \Rightarrow \omega t_2=\frac{\pi}{2} \\ t_2 & =\frac{\pi}{2 \omega} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore$$ Minimum time taken by current to reach its peak value from rms value

$$\begin{aligned} & =t_2-t_1=\frac{\pi}{2 \omega}-\frac{\pi}{4 \omega}=\frac{\pi}{4 \omega} \\ & =\frac{\pi}{4 \times 2 \times \pi \times 50}=\frac{1}{400}=2.5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~s} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: The trajectory of a projectile projected from origin is given by the equation $$y=x-\frac{2 x^2}{5}$$. The initial velocity of the projectile is
en.explanation:
The trajectory of projectile projected from aigin is given as $$y=x-\frac{2 x^2}{5}\quad \text{..... (i)}$$

comparing Eq (i) with trajectory of projectile

$$y=x \tan \theta-\frac{g}{2 u^2 \cos ^2 \theta} x^2$$

we get, $$\tan \theta=1-\tan 45^{\circ}$$

$$\therefore \quad \theta=45^{\circ} \text { (Angle of projection) }$$

when, $$x=R$$, then $$y=H=0$$

$$\therefore$$ from Eq (i)

$$\begin{aligned} 0 & =R-\frac{2 R^2}{5} \\ 0 & =R\left(1-\frac{2 R}{5}\right) \Rightarrow R \neq 0 \\ \therefore \quad 1-\frac{2 R}{5} & =0 \Rightarrow R=\frac{5}{2} \end{aligned}$$

Where $$R=$$ Range of Projectile

$$\begin{gathered} \frac{u^2 \sin 2 \times 45^{\circ}}{9}=\frac{5}{2} \quad \left[g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right]\\ u^2=\frac{5}{2} \times 10 \Rightarrow u=5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \end{gathered}$$

en.content: An object with mass $$5 \mathrm{~kg}$$ is acted upon by a force, $$\mathbf{F}=(-3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}) \mathrm{N}$$. If its initial velocity at $$t=0$$ is $$\mathbf{v}=(3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+12 \hat{\mathbf{j}}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$$, the time at which it will just have a velocity along $$y$$-axis is -
en.explanation:
Given, Mass of object, $$m=5 \mathrm{~kg}$$

$$\mathbf{F}=(-3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{j}} \mathbf{N}$$

Initial velocity, at $$t=0$$

$$\mathbf{v}=(3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+12 \mathbf{j}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$$

If $$t$$ be the time at which object have a velocity along $$y$$-axis, then at time $$t, \mathrm{v}_x=0$$

at time, $$t=0, \mathbf{u}_x=3$$

$$\therefore$$ acceleration along $$x$$-direction

$$a_x=\frac{F_x}{m}=\frac{-3}{5}\quad$$ [retarded motion]

$$\therefore$$ From equation of motion

$$\begin{aligned} & \mathbf{v}_x=u_x+a_x t \\ & 0=3-\left(\frac{3}{5}\right) t \Rightarrow t=5 \mathrm{~s} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: During inelastic collision between two objects, which of the following quantity always remains conserved?
en.explanation:
Total linear momentum is always conserved in all type of collision.

$$\therefore$$ During inelastic collision, total linear momentum is conserved but total kinetic energy and total mechanical energy is not conserved.

en.content: In Rutherford experiment, for head-on collision of $$\alpha$$-particles with a gold nucleus, the impact parameter is

From Eq (i),

$$b=0$$

en.content: Frequency of revolution of an electron revolving in $$n$$th orbit of $$\mathrm{H}$$-atom is proportional to
en.explanation:
Time period of revolving electron in $$n$$th orbit of $$\mathrm{H}$$-atom,

$$\begin{gathered} T_n=\frac{2 \pi r_n}{v_n} \\ T_n \propto \frac{r_n}{v_n} \quad \text{... (i)} \end{gathered}$$

where, $$r_n \rightarrow$$ radius of $$n$$th orbit

$$v_n \rightarrow$$ yelocity of electron in $$n$$th orbit

$$\therefore$$ From Eq (i),

$$T_n \propto \frac{n^2}{1 / n} \Rightarrow T_n \propto n^3$$

$$\therefore$$ Frequency of electron in $$n$$th orbit

$$\begin{aligned} & f_n \propto \frac{1}{T_n} \\ & f_n \propto \frac{1}{n^3} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A hydrogen atom is ground state absorbs $$10.2 \mathrm{~eV}$$ of energy. The orbital angular momentum of the electron is increased by

en.content: The end product of decay of $${ }_{90} \mathrm{Th}^{232}$$ is $${ }_{82} \mathrm{~Pb}^{208}$$. The number of $$\alpha$$ and $$\beta$$ particles emitted are respectively
en.explanation:

Number of emitted $$\alpha$$-particle $$=\frac{24}{4}=6$$

$$=90-82=8$$

On emission of $$6 \alpha$$-particle, atomic number decreases by 12 units.

$$\therefore$$ number of emitted $$\beta$$-particle

$$=12-8=4$$

en.content: A particle is moving uniformly along a straight line as shown in the figure. During the motion of the particle from $$A$$ to $$B$$, the angular momentum of the particle about $$O$$
en.explanation:
The angular momentum of a particle moving uniformly along a straight line about a point $ O $ can be analyzed through the concept of cross product $ \mathbf{L} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p} $, where $ \mathbf{L} $ is the angular momentum, $ \mathbf{r} $ is the position vector from the point $ O $ to the particle, and $ \mathbf{p} $ is the linear momentum of the particle.

Given the uniform motion along the line from $ A $ to $ B $:

Since the direction and magnitude of the motion remain constant,

As the particle moves from $ A $ to $ B $, its distance from point $ O $ changes.

If the distance between $ O $ and the line of motion is constant, then the perpendicular distance from $ O $ to the particle's line of motion remains the same, keeping the angular momentum constant.

Therefore, the angular momentum of the particle about point $ O $ during its motion from $ A $ to $ B $ remains constant.

Option C: remains constant

en.content: A satellite is orbiting close to the earth and has a kinetic energy $$K$$. The minimum extra kinetic energy required by it just overcome the gravitation pull of the earth is
en.explanation:
Kinetic energy of satellite revolving close to the earth

$$\begin{aligned} & K=\frac{1}{2} m \cdot v_0^2=\frac{1}{2} m(\sqrt{g R})^2 \quad\left[v_0=\sqrt{g R}\right] \\ & K=\frac{1}{2} m g R \end{aligned}$$

Escape energy near the earth surface

$$\begin{aligned} K_e & =\frac{1}{2} m \cdot v_e^2 \quad\left[v_e \rightarrow \text { escape velocity }\right] \\ & =\frac{1}{2} m(\sqrt{2 g R})^2=m g R=2 \times \frac{1}{2} m g R=2 K \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore$$ Minimum extra kinetic energy to overcome gravitational pull $$=K_e-K=2 K-K=K$$

en.content: A wire is stretched such that its volume remains constant. The poission's ratio of the material of the wire is
en.explanation:
Volume of wire is given by $$V=\pi r^2 l\quad \text{.... (i)}$$

where, $$r=$$ radius of wire

$$\quad l=$$ length of wire

Since, volume of wire is constant, hence

$$d v=0\quad \text{.... (ii)}$$

From Eq (i)

$$\begin{aligned} & \frac{d V}{V}=2 \frac{d r}{r}+\frac{d l}{l} \\ & 0=2 \frac{d r}{r}+\frac{d l}{l} \end{aligned}$$

$$-\frac{d r}{r}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{d l}{l} \Rightarrow \frac{\frac{d r}{r}}{\frac{d l}{l}}=-\frac{1}{2}$$

$$\therefore$$ Poission's ratio, $$\sigma=\frac{d r / r}{d l / l}=-\frac{1}{2}=-0.5$$

en.content: A cylindrical container containing water has a small hole at height of $$H=8 \mathrm{~cm}$$ from the bottom and at a depth of $$2 \mathrm{~cm}$$ from the top surface of the liquid. The maximum horizontal distance travelled by the water before it hits the ground $$x$$ is

en.content: A transparent medium shows relation between $$i$$ and $$r$$ as shown. If the speed of light in vacuum is $$c$$, the Brewster angle for the medium is
en.explanation:

But, by Brewster's law

en.content: If Young's double slit experiment, using monochromatic light of wavelength $$\lambda$$, the intensity of light at a point on the screen where path difference is $$\lambda$$ is $$K$$ units. The intensity of light at a point where path difference is $$\frac{\lambda}{3}$$ is
en.explanation:
The intensity at any point on the screen in Young's double slit experiment $$K=I_0 \cos ^2 \frac{\phi}{2}\quad \text{.... (i)}$$

where, $$I_0$$ is intensity of either source.

when, path difference $$=\lambda$$

then, phase difference $$\phi=2 \pi$$, then from Eq. (i)

$$\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad K & =I_0 \cos ^2 \frac{2 \pi}{2}=I_0(-1)^2 \\ K & =I_0 \quad \text{.... (ii)} \end{aligned}$$

when, path difference $$=\frac{\lambda}{3}$$

then path difference, $$\phi=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \times$$ path difference

$$=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \times \frac{\lambda}{3}=\frac{2 \pi}{3}$$

$$\therefore$$ From Eq (i), $$I^{\prime}=I \cos ^2\left(\frac{\frac{2 \pi}{3}}{2}\right)=I_0 \cos ^2 \frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{I_0}{4}=\frac{K}{4}$$

en.content: Due to Doppler's effect the shift in wavelength observed is $$0.1 \mathop A\limits^o$$ for a star producing wavelength $$6000 \mathop A\limits^o$$. Velocity of recession of the star will be
en.explanation:
Given, Doppler's shift, $$\Delta \lambda=0 \mathrm{l}\mathop A\limits^o$$

$$=0.1 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{~m}=10^{-11} \mathrm{~m}$$

wavelength, $$\lambda=6000 \mathop A\limits^o=6 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$$

If $$v_s$$ is the velocity of recession of the star and $$c$$ is velocity of light, then Doppler's shift

$$\begin{aligned} \Delta \lambda =\left(\frac{v_s}{c}\right) \lambda \Rightarrow v_s=\frac{c \cdot \Delta \lambda}{\lambda}=\frac{3 \times 10^8 \times 10^{-11}}{6 \times 10^{-7}} \\ =0.5 \times 10^4=5 \times 10^3 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}=5 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: An electron is moving with an initial velocity $$\mathbf{v}=v_0 \hat{\mathbf{i}}$$ and is in a uniform magnetic field $$\mathbf{B}=B_0 \hat{\mathbf{j}}$$. Then its de-Broglie wavelength
en.explanation:
Initial velocity of electron $$\mathbf{v}=v_0 \hat{\mathbf{i}}$$

Magnetic field, $$\mathbf{B}=B_0 \hat{\mathbf{j}}$$, when electron is moving in perpendicular direction of magnetic field, than it moves on circular path, and radius $$r$$ of circular path is given by $$r=\frac{m v_0}{B_0 e}$$

$$\Rightarrow \quad r=\frac{p}{B_0 e}$$

Where, $$p=$$ momentum. $$p=r B_0 e$$

$$\therefore$$ de-Broglie wavelength associated with electron is

$$\lambda=\frac{h}{p}=\frac{h}{r B_0 e}$$

Since, $$h$$ and $$e$$ are constant and $$r$$ is also constant for constant $$B_0$$. Hence, de-Broglie wavelength associated with electron remains constant.

en.content: Light of certain frequency and intensity incident on a photosensitive material causes photoelectric effect. If both the frequency and intensity are doubled, the photoelectric saturation current becomes
en.explanation:
Photoelectric saturation current $$i$$ does not depend on frequency of incident radiation but it is directly proportional to the intensity $$I$$ of incident radiation.

$$\begin{array}{ll}\text { i.e. } \quad & i \propto I \\ \text { i.e. } \quad & \frac{i_1}{i_2}=\frac{I_1}{I_2}\end{array}$$

when, $$\quad I_2=2 I_1$$

then, $$\quad \frac{i_1}{i_2}=\frac{I_1}{2 I_1} \Rightarrow i_2=2 i_1$$

en.content: A certain charge $$2 Q$$ is divided at first into two parts $$q_1$$ and $$q_2$$. Later the charges are placed at a certain distance. If the force of interaction between two chagrges is maximum then $$\frac{Q}{q_1}$$ is
en.explanation:

en.content: A particle of mass $$m$$ and charge $$q$$ is placed at rest in uniform electric field $$E$$ and then released. The kinetic energy attained by the particle after moving a distance $$y$$ is
en.explanation:
When a charge particle of mass $$m$$ and charge $$q$$ is released in the uniform electric field, then it is accelerated in the direction of electric field,

$$\therefore$$ Acceleration of the charge particle, $$a=\frac{F}{m}, a=\frac{q E}{m}$$

$$[\because F=q E]$$

$$\therefore$$ Final velocity of electron at a distance $$y$$ is given by

$$\begin{aligned} & v^2=u^2+2 a y=0+2 \cdot \frac{q E}{m} \cdot y \\ & v^2=\frac{2 q E y}{m} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore$$ Kinetic energy $$\mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m v^2=\frac{1}{2} m \cdot \frac{2 q E y}{m}=E q y$$

en.content: A system of two charges separated by a certain distance apart stores electrical potential energy. If the distance between them is increased, the potential energy of the system

en.content: An inductor of inductance $$L$$ and resistor $$R$$ are joined together in series and connected by a source of frequency $$\omega$$. The power dissipated in the circuit is
en.explanation:

en.content: A certain prism is found to produce a minimum deviation of $$38^{\circ}$$. It produce a deviation of $$44^{\circ}$$ when the angle of incidence is either $$42^{\circ}$$ or $$62^{\circ}$$. What is the angle of incidence when it is undergoing minimum deviation?

en.content: An aluminium sphere is dipped into water. Which of the following is true?

options.content: Buoyancy will be less in water at $$0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$$ than that is water at $$4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$$
Buoyancy will be more in water at $$0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$$ than that in water at $$4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$$
Buoyancy in water at $$0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$$ will be same as that in water at $$4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$$
Buoyancy may be more or less in water $$4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$$ depending on the radius of the sphere

en.explanation: Buoyancy depends on the fluid in which the body is immersed. More the density, more is the buoyancy, since density of water at $$4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$$ is maximum, so the buoyancy at $$4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$$ will be maximum. So, (a) is correct.

en.content: One mole of $$\mathrm{O}_2$$ gas is heated at constant pressure starting at $$27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$$. How much energy must be added to the gas as to double its volume?
en.explanation:
As heated at constant. pressure, using Charle's law $$\frac{V_1}{V_2}=\frac{T_1}{T_2}$$

here $$\quad V_2=2 V_1, T_1=27^{\circ}=27+273=300 \mathrm{~K}$$

$$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{2}=\frac{300}{T_2} \Rightarrow T_2=600 \mathrm{~K}$$

Now, energy to be added

$$\begin{aligned} \Delta U & =n C_p\left(T_2-T_1\right)=1 \times \frac{7}{2} \times R \times 300 \\ & =1050 R \end{aligned}$$
